title: The judge's chair
summary: Leave the debater's chair for the judge's one: find out what a ballot is really asking, watch a recorded round from outside it with a pen moving, and write and deliver your first reason for decision. Then the Expedition dossier opens and the talk that closes the whole arc gets its shape.
materials: last season's hand-ruled ballot, or a fresh one ruled the same way
a recorded debate round to judge, on any screen
poster board and markers for the Expedition dossier

steps.title: What a judge is actually doing
steps.body:
For a year you have been the one talking. Today you sit in the other chair, and it is harder than it looks from where you have been sitting.

A ballot is not a scorecard for a performance. It does not ask who was louder, funnier, faster or more sure of themselves. It asks one question: which side won the argument that actually happened in that room. Not the argument you would have run. The one they ran.

Three words you need before you can fill one in.

Clash. The place two cases actually collide. They say the cost is too high, the other side says the cost is worth it, and now there is something for somebody to decide. Two speeches that never touch each other are two speeches, not a debate. From inside a round clash is hard to spot, because you are busy. From the judge's chair it is most of what there is to see.

Weighing. When both sides are partly right, and they usually are, the judge decides which of the two things matters more, and says why. That sentence is the whole job. A judge who will not weigh has not judged, they have only described.

The RFD, which is short for the reason for decision. It is not a summary of what happened. It is an argument for your own verdict, and it can be a bad one, which is exactly why it gets said out loud.

One thing that is allowed to feel strange, and it is the real lesson of the chair. You can think a side is right and still vote against them, because they did not argue it. The gap between what is true and what got argued is where judging lives.

The question of the week runs underneath all of it: when you judge, whose side are you on? Answer it in your own words at the end of your recording, and take your time, because the honest answer is not the obvious one.

steps.title: Judge a recorded round, and write the RFD
steps.body:
A grown-up picks the round and you do not, because choosing which round to judge is already a kind of judging.

Any recording works: one of yours from last season, or, if nothing suitable survives, two grown-ups record a three minute round on the spot with one argument each per side.

Watch it once, cold, with the ballot in front of you and the pen moving the whole time. Not notes about who you liked. Two columns, each side's points written down as they are made, and a tick in the answered box only when somebody actually replied to a point rather than talking past it.

At the end, before you decide anything at all, do the thing that makes this hard: draw a circle around the one row where the two sides genuinely collided. If there is no such row, that is a real finding and you say so out loud.

Then write the RFD by hand. Three sentences and no more.

The first names the clash. The round came down to whether the cost was worth it.

The second weighs it. I found the cost argument the stronger one, because they gave a number and the other side only said it felt like too much.

The third is the verdict, and it names a winner. Nothing hedged, no both sides did well.

Two rules for this first one. Nothing about delivery, voice or nerves gets written down; a ballot is about arguments and only arguments. And if you were in the round yourself, say so at the top and judge it anyway, which is harder and considerably more interesting than it sounds.

Then read it aloud to whoever is in the room, standing up, the way a real judge announces one.
checklist: A grown-up chose the round, not me
The ballot was filled in while the round played, not from memory afterwards
I circled the one row where the sides actually collided, or said out loud that there was not one
Three sentences: the clash, the weighing, the verdict, and nothing about anybody's voice
I read it aloud standing up

steps.title: The Expedition dossier opens
steps.body:
The season ends in an event you design and you run, and the waiting is half of what makes it good, so the board goes up today and fills all summer.

Take a poster board and title it The Grand Expedition. Nothing on it gets decided today except its shape.

Four headings down the left side: Talk. Stations. Guests. Run of show.

Under Talk, write the only thing that is fixed. Ten minutes, four acts, one act per season. Act one is the forest, act two the coast, act three the mountains, act four this desert. You draft and perform one act at each summit, so by the last week you will already have stood inside every part of the longest speech you have ever given, and nothing will be new on the day except the running order.

Leave the rest of the board empty on purpose. What the talk is actually about is not on it yet. That decision is yours, it comes later, and nobody else is going to make it for you.

One rule for the board: anything that occurs to you in any week goes on it the same day, in pencil. Ideas that wait for a good moment do not survive the week.
checklist: The board is up somewhere I walk past it
Four headings on it, with only the talk's shape filled in
I can say what the four acts are, in order, without reading them off the board

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the RFD delivered standing, three sentences, the way a judge announces one. Then say which row you circled as the clash and why you weighed it the way you did. Finish with your own answer to the question of the week: when you judge, whose side are you on?
